bottle.name: Auchentoshan 12 Year Old Double Cask Single Malt Scotch Whisky
bottle.mash: Malted barley alone, as the law asks of any single malt Scotch whisky.
bottle.still: Distilled three times at Clydebank, through a wash still, an intermediate still and a spirit still, which by the house's account carry the spirit to about 81 per cent alcohol, against about 70 for two distillations.
bottle.wood: Twelve years in American oak casks that held bourbon and Spanish oak casks that held Oloroso sherry, by the house's account. The age statement is twelve years.
bottle.taste: Sweet pastry, a burst of citrus, nuttiness and a green, leafy note on the nose, then lemon zest and oak, tangerine and lime, and a sharp finish of ginger.
bottle.pour: Neat or with a little water, or tall with soda; the house also stirs it into a Manhattan, where it reads light and citrus.

label.means: Matured in two kinds of cask: American oak that held bourbon and Spanish oak that held Oloroso sherry.
Each whisky in it has had twelve years or longer in oak.

records.table: Three distillations, not the usual two, make Auchentoshan 12 Year Old Double Cask light and clean, with citrus, sweet pastry and nuts from bourbon and Oloroso sherry casks; it is made at Clydebank on the edge of Glasgow. Sip it neat, or top it with soda for a highball.
records.story: The distillery took out its licence in 1823 on land near Duntocher, west of Glasgow; some accounts trace a still on the site a few years earlier, under the Duntocher name. Auchentoshan, the name it took, means the corner of the field in Gaelic. Through the nineteenth century and much of the twentieth it passed from one owner to the next. On 13 and 14 March 1941 the German raids remembered as the Clydebank Blitz struck the town: three of the distillery's warehouses were destroyed with the whisky in them, and, as the story goes, a bomb crater behind the site became the pond that holds its cooling water. In 1984 the whisky firm later named Morrison Bowmore Distillers bought the distillery, and in 1994 Suntory took full control of that company. Whoever held it, the three stills stayed the point, a habit once shared by other Lowland houses and kept here for all of the spirit. The 12 Year Old turns triple distillation into something a guest can taste: light in a highball, and with enough sherry cask in it to stand up in a Manhattan.

others.name: Auchentoshan American Oak

traps: Triple distillation is the house's habit, not a Lowland rule: the regulations ask nothing of the stills, and most Lowland malt is distilled twice.
Clydebank sits on the Clyde by Glasgow, south of the Highland line, so Auchentoshan is a Lowland malt and not a Highland one.
In 2025 the house put out the 12 Year Old Double Cask, from bourbon and Oloroso sherry casks, in place of its 12 Year Old; older bottles read only 12 Year Old.

bottle.name: Glenkinchie 12 Year Old Single Malt Scotch Whisky
bottle.mash: Malted barley alone, as the law asks of a single malt; the producer names no barley variety.
bottle.still: Distilled in copper pot stills at Pencaitland, the spirit condensed in a cast-iron worm tub, a coil of copper pipe sunk in cold water, which the producer credits with giving the spirit more character and depth.

records.table: The Lowland house of the Classic Malts stands at Pencaitland in East Lothian, near Edinburgh, and Glenkinchie 12 Year Old is its gentle glass: vanilla, cut flowers and lemon at 43% ABV. Before dinner it wants nothing more than a little water.
records.story: By the account most often told, two brothers of the Rate family, farmers, began distilling at or near the site around 1825 under the name Milton. No record joins the two names for certain, though Milton is held likely to be Glenkinchie under its first name, and the house itself counts its years from 1825. The Rates were licensed as Glenkinchie in 1837. In the 1890s the distillery was rebuilt as a model Victorian distillery. In 1914 Glenkinchie joined Rosebank, St Magdalene, Grange and Clydesdale, five Lowland houses together, to form Scottish Malt Distillers, and in 1925 the Distillers Company bought that firm. For decades its malt went into blends. In the late 1980s it was chosen as the Lowland house of the Classic Malts, a range that set one malt from each region side by side. Its 12 Year Old gives the Lowland style in brief: vanilla, lemon and flowers, and nothing heavy.

records.table: The River Bladnoch runs beside the Galloway distillery, near Wigtown, that makes Bladnoch 10 Year Old: bourbon cask malt at 46.7% ABV, not chill filtered, with honey, citrus and a peppery bite. It was distilled before the stills fell silent in 2009.
records.story: Bladnoch began in 1817 as a licensed farm distillery on the River Bladnoch near Wigtown, in Galloway, founded by two brothers of a farming family. Closings and returns marked the years that followed. In the twentieth century it fell silent and was revived more than once, and it passed through the hands of the big blending groups. A private buyer took it from United Distillers in 1994 and brought it back into production in 2000. Distilling stopped again in 2009, and in 2014 the business failed and the distillery was put up for sale. In July 2015 an Australian businessman bought it. In January 2017, its two-hundredth year, the first bottlings of the revival were announced, Samsara, Adela and Talia, all drawn on whisky made before the silence, and later that year distilling began again. The 10 Year Old followed, matured in bourbon casks alone and bottled at 46.7% ABV without chill filtering, a clear picture of the old Bladnoch spirit before the new stills had whisky of their own to give. Light, honeyed and fresh, it is the Galloway malt from a distillery that has come back from closure more than once.

bottle.name: Kingsbarns Doocot Single Malt Scotch Whisky
bottle.mash: Malted barley alone, grown on farms in Fife and malted without peat, by the house's account.
bottle.still: Distilled slowly in two copper pot stills made by Forsyths of Rothes, by the house's account, at the distillery in a restored farm steading on the Cambo Estate.

records.table: Named in Scots for the old dovecote on its farm, Kingsbarns Doocot is the flagship of a young Lowland distillery near St Andrews in Fife: first-fill bourbon barrels with a touch of red wine barrique, and banana, pineapple and summer berries in the glass.
records.story: The idea began with a local golf caddie, who heard visitors to the courses of Fife ask for a distillery nearby and found there was none. He planned one in the derelict farm steading of East Newhall, on the Cambo Estate, buildings put up around 1800 about a castellated dovecote. By 2013 the family behind the bottling house Wemyss Malts had taken the project over, keeping the caddie on as a director, and the distillery opened in November 2014, its first casks filled soon after. The first single malt, Dream to Dram, followed: mostly first-fill bourbon barrels, with a tenth of red wine barriques. On 3 March 2023 Doocot took its place as the flagship, by the house's account the same spirit and the same casks, left longer in oak, and Dream to Dram was retired. Doocot is what the new Lowland tastes like: Fife barley, no peat, and fruit where the older Lowland houses give grass.

records.table: Lindores MCDXCIV wears in Roman numerals the year 1494, when an Exchequer entry shows malt sent to a friar to make aqua vitae, an entry the distillery ties to the ruined abbey it stands beside, at Newburgh in Fife. In the glass, vanilla, orchard fruit and citrus.
records.story: Lindores Abbey was founded in 1191, a house of the Tironensian monks on the edge of Newburgh, by the Firth of Tay. In the Exchequer Rolls for 1494 stands an entry of eight bolls of malt given to a friar by order of the king, wherewith to make aqua vitae. Historians of whisky tell it as the start of its written history in Scotland, and the distillery tells the friar as a monk of Lindores, though other accounts place him elsewhere, and whether he distilled there is not known. The abbey fell to ruin and its lands became farms. The family who farmed beside the ruins set out to bring distilling back, and the distillery, built beside the abbey, first ran spirit in December 2017. Members of its 1494 Society received the first bottles of single malt in 2021, and on 2 July 2021 Lindores MCDXCIV went on general sale. At the table the bottle tells its own story: a young Lowland malt from beside the abbey that whisky history ties to the record of 1494.
